item.title: At Tree 55, Vietnam’s Gen Z Demands to Hold the Privileged Accountable
item.description:
A young woman in a red hoodie and wide sunglasses stopped her motorbike just past Tree 55 on Nguyen Huy Tu Street in central Hanoi. She snapped a photo with her phone. She stared at the tree again. She lingered with defiance.

No one else was parked there at lunchtime on Tuesday in front of the quiet men in pairs with hints of plainclothes authority — the middle-manager dress shoes, the aviator shades.

Tree 55, as everyone likely knew, was where an 18-year-old student, Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, better known as Mina, had been hit along with her father by a BMW. She died after being thrown from a motorbike just days before her university exams. That was 15 months ago.

I was there this week to see whether flowers would arrive. The bright bouquets teens and twenty-somethings kept delivering, photographing and sharing on social media. The ones the police had recently removed. And if tension hovered in their absence, it was with good reason.

On Monday night, after an eruption of Gen Z outrage and creativity thrust Memorial Tree 55, or “The Tree of Justice,” into the local zeitgeist, Vietnam’s national broadcaster officially confirmed what many had long insisted: A former Communist Party official, Nguyen Sy Cuong, had been behind the wheel of that BMW.

The TV report said Mr. Cuong — who had been vice chairman of the foreign affairs committee in the National Assembly until earlier this year — caused the crash by illegally driving on the wrong side of the road. It also said that he was not prosecuted because he had compensated the victim’s relatives, and they chose not to press charges. The victim’s father, with his face obscured, urged people to move on in the segment, which did not mention that Mr. Cuong’s wife is Vietnam’s minister of culture, sports and tourism.

Their powerful positions, some said, had kept the crash out of public view.

But in a one-party state that Harvard scholars have described as repressive but responsive, the official acknowledgment of responsibility was an extraordinary concession to public pressure. Warning against “opportunists exploiting the incident on social media,” the report reflected the government’s deep concerns about an unexpected youth movement pushing for accountability at a time when officials are focused on economic growth.

Adding to the sensitivity, the collective action comes after Gen Z activists toppled leaders in Nepal, challenged authorities in Indonesia, and continue to rattle the power structure in India.

Hanoi officials had already warned state-run outlets to reduce coverage of the youth-driven “Cockroach” demonstrations rocking New Delhi, according to a written notice shared among reporters. The internal guidance said that the information could be “exploited for anti-government purposes.”

And yet, for now at least, Monday’s careful admissions in TV form show no sign of weakening the resistance to what many see as sloppy propaganda and protection for the powerful.

On Wednesday, legal experts said the victim’s family could not, simply by declining to press charges, determine whether Mr. Cuong would be prosecuted. Online, anonymous critics accused the state broadcaster of using A.I. to doctor a document showing Mr. Cuong had passed a sobriety test. Others questioned if it was really the victim’s father in the report.

Their claims could not be independently verified. The network did not respond to requests for comment. Mr. Cuong, reached by phone on Wednesday, said only “I am busy, I cannot talk” before hanging up.

By midafternoon, the original version of the news report had disappeared from YouTube.

And all that public anger is about more than the crash. It reflects a broader frustration with corruption, privilege and the mechanisms of secrecy that benefit elites in a fast-changing society that has become more bifurcated by wealth and political connections.

As one commenter wrote on Threads on Wednesday, letting Mr. Cuong sidestep criminal prosecution simply confirms that the country’s legal system “creates loopholes so that the rich can stuff money and power into them, while the poor cannot.”

Fury over who gets to police both behavior and expression has also fueled the backlash. Censorship, in fact, sparked its rise.

On July 31, a rapper known as MCK announced that he would scrub digital platforms of several songs that cultural authorities had deemed vulgar from his new hit album.

That’s when Mr. Cuong’s wife, Lam Thi Phuong Thanh, the minister of culture since April, became a target of especially intense curiosity.

Within days of MCK’s cleanup, Threads lit up with questions about why there was so little information made public about the crash on May 25, 2025, involving her husband.

On Aug. 12, Luat Khoa, an independent Vietnamese news outlet run by former reporters for state-run media who have mostly left the country, reported that Nguyen Sy Cuong had become one of the platform’s top topics, with more than 1 million posts related to the accident.

The next day, a Facebook page about Vietnamese politics posted an announcement saying that the authorities had requested that Facebook “continuously block three of my posts about Nguyen Sy Cuong.”

Then security video from a nearby building surfaced and started to spread online.

It showed the BMW, an SUV, smashing into the tree with a motorbike against its grill. A man gets out, seemingly uninjured, and can be seen approaching where Mina and her father have been thrown. A woman bearing a strong resemblance to Ms. Thanh emerges from the passenger side as a crowd gathers. She heads away from the scene, comes back to collect something from the front seat, then walks away.

In the brief clip, neither driver nor passenger rushed to help the wounded.

Another eruption of social media outrage followed, with some quoting “Animal Farm,” and “The Hunger Games,” accusing Ms. Thanh of trying to protect herself and her husband after online takedown orders spread to more posts.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Threads, did not respond to a request for comment. Its most recent report on Vietnam shows a rise in censorship, with restrictions placed on more than 5,300 items in the last six months of 2025 in response to requests from the Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Public Security.

Undeterred, people found other ways to make their sadness and anger known. They ordered flowers to be delivered to the base of Tree 55. Users posted photos of a growing, colorful pile until the afternoon of Aug. 14, when another set of images made the rounds — showing the bouquets being removed by the police and thrown into a dumpster.

Then the Threads community turned to white ribbons, tying them on backpacks, as symbols of student promise.

Around the same time, someone created a virtual Memorial Tree Number 55.

“Rest in peace down there, sister,” said one of the many notes left at the site. “We Gen-Z will handle everything.”

The government has yet to mention or cut off access to the collection.

Ms. Thanh could not be reached for comment on Wednesday. She and her husband did not appear in the state television report — a point some critics interpreted as a lack of remorse.

In the void, messages of support for Mina and calls for accountability continue to multiply.

Tung Ngo contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump vs. the International Criminal Court
item.description:
President Trump has never liked the International Criminal Court. In his first term, he called it a “threat” to American sovereignty. Secretary of State Marco Rubio this week accused it of being “corrupt and fatally politicized.”

But the administration hasn’t stopped at words. After announcing sanctions on the court’s chief prosecutor and nine of its judges this year, the Trump administration this week imposed sanctions on the court’s president and senior trial lawyer, too.

To its detractors, the court attempts to exercise illegitimate authority over sovereign nations; to its supporters, it’s a powerful symbol of the rules-based international order that the Trump administration has sought to undermine. Today, my colleague Amanda Taub writes about whether it can survive the Trump era, and why that matters.

By Amanda Taub

The United States has always had a tricky relationship with the International Criminal Court, which tries people accused of war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

It helped create the court but never joined the tribunal, partly because of fears that such a move would expose Americans, especially those in the military, to politically motivated prosecutions. Many U.S. politicians, particularly on the right, have treated it as a threat.

And yet at times, the U.S. has been one of the court’s most important partners. It has provided intelligence, diplomatic assistance and other support when doing so served U.S. interests. The Biden administration provided crucial help in the court’s investigation of Russian actions in Ukraine, for example.

Under the Trump administration, however, the relationship has shifted from complicated to outright hostile.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on the president of the court, as well as a senior trial lawyer in the prosecutor’s office. That brings the total number of court officials under U.S. sanctions to 13, including half of its judges.

Rubio has gone even further, announcing that the U.S. intends to dismantle the I.C.C. — “brick by brick, if necessary” — including by pressuring member states to leave the court. Within days of that announcement last month, Venezuela announced its exit, followed by Chad.

The Trump administration’s targeting of an international institution is not new. But the I.C.C. seems particularly vulnerable.

The court is almost entirely dependent on a delicate, consensus-based system of norms to do its work. The Trump administration has often been actively hostile to that system, let alone any suggestion that the U.S. should abide by its rules.

The pressure on the court has risen sharply in Trump’s second term, after it issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and at least one other Israeli official. The I.C.C. has also been rocked by a sexual misconduct scandal involving its former chief prosecutor. That raises a very real question: Can the I.C.C. survive the Trump era?

A court dependent on cooperation

The I.C.C. has no police force and no subpoena powers. Its investigators cannot visit crime sites to gather evidence without permission from the country where the sites are located. It can detain suspects only if they willingly surrender, or if states arrest them on the court’s behalf. And it relies on member states for its funding.

The result is that the I.C.C. can function effectively only when states cooperate. Member states have a treaty obligation to assist the court, but if they don’t, there is little the I.C.C. can do. And yet until now, states have often helped the court — because international norms demanded it, and because the reputational harm of refusing would be severe.

Now, the U.S. is taking direct aim at those norms.

Venezuela, for example, remained a member state after the I.C.C. prosecutor’s decision in 2021 to investigate whether its government had committed crimes against humanity. So observers took note when it withdrew last month — perhaps because of U.S. pressure, or because the U.S. assault on the court gave its leaders cover, or possibly some combination of the two.

“Some countries that might otherwise support the court will now find it too costly to do so,” if the U.S. imposes consequences on those that remain, said Kate Cronin-Furman, who studies human rights in international affairs. Others that already wanted to pull out may now find it easier.

Countries that strongly support the I.C.C.’s mission, and oppose Trump’s foreign policy, will probably increase their support for the court, she said.

But that support may not help in the long run. One of the biggest challenges for the I.C.C. has been combating the perception — held by the Trump administration, among others — that it’s just another vehicle for politics. That challenge will only grow if the I.C.C. comes to be seen as an anti-Trump institution, rather than a neutral arbiter of justice.

A small part of a big project

If the I.C.C. is damaged or even destroyed, the world won’t feel the consequences immediately. The court, which handles long and complex investigations, has tried only a small number of cases since its founding in 2002. Regardless of the I.C.C.’s fate, most perpetrators of atrocities will never end up in its courtroom.

But the indirect consequences, for the cause of international justice and the principles of the international order, would be more significant, experts say.

The I.C.C. is a small but important part of a broader project that says that the conduct of international affairs should be guided by laws and rules, rather than simply power. It’s a project the Trump administration has long argued ties the hands of one of the world’s most powerful countries.

Countries around the world were already “de-prioritizing” their commitments to international justice, said Alex Whiting, a Harvard law professor. That is partly because of other, more pressing issues, such as Europe’s need to increase its defense spending. But there is also more general loss of faith in international solutions and institutions, he said.

Because the court is an organization built on belief — in trust in a now-fading system — there may ultimately be no need for the Trump administration to dismantle it brick by brick. It has already undermined the structures that made the I.C.C. possible; if they start to collapse, that might well be enough.

The U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, starting a war that has spread to neighboring countries, halted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and rattled the global economy.

As the conflict nears the six-month mark, we want to hear from our readers.

What questions do you have about the state of the war? Are you concerned about its impact near you? Are you wondering about the options for Washington, Tehran, or other countries in the region? Send us your questions and we will take them to our correspondents in the Middle East, the U.S. and elsewhere.

Israel’s military will open criminal investigations into the killing of some Palestinians by its troops in Gaza, including the death of a 5-year-old girl.

The United Arab Emirates is halting all trade with Iran as the Trump administration tries yet again to ramp up economic pressure on Iran.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s popular young defense minister who was fired by President Volodymyr Zelensky last month, called for elections.

A new mRNA vaccine could prevent skin cancer from returning, Moderna and Merck said.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. showed signs of progress ahead of an extended tariff deadline set for midnight on Friday.

After a Gen Z outcry in Vietnam, the government said that a former Communist Party official was behind a car crash that killed a teenager.

Cecilia Kang, who covers technology for The Times, traveled to the “data center capital of the world” outside Washington to see how the A.I. boom is affecting the area. Watch her video.

Aliko Dangote is Africa’s richest man. He is more than $5 billion richer these days thanks in part to the war in Iran.

Guo Degang, one of China’s best-known comedians, is under investigation for riffing on the lyrics of a patriotic song.

In a new video, Queen Camilla talked about how hard it had been to keep King Charles III’s cancer diagnosis secret.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about the death of the Cambridge professor Jason Arday.

Tennis: Nick Kyrgios, a one-time Wimbledon finalist, tested positive for cocaine at an ATP Tour event.

Natalie Harp is always by Trump’s side. The White House aide never takes a day off. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She has written him letters and concluded one with the above sign-off. Last week, she was revealed as one of the lucky few who joined the president on his secret flight out of Turkey. So, what exactly does she do?

If you had imagined 20 years ago what Shania Twain’s audience would look like today, you might have pictured something middle-aged. But at Wembley Stadium in London this summer, where she opened for Harry Styles, there were gaggles of girls and women of all varieties — moms and daughters, glitter-covered teenagers, young professionals in cosplay — and plenty of leopard print.

Twain’s young fans often see her as a glamorous, self-actualized champion whose songs are explicitly feminist statements. There’s only one wrinkle: Twain does not entirely identify with all of this. Read the interview.

Football is big business, and while the women’s game still lags in ticket sales and attendance, the gap is closing. In fact, women’s football is predicted to become a top-five global sport by the end of this decade. “Women’s sports are part of this cultural zeitgeist,” one expert said.

The latest season of “Ted Lasso,” the popular Apple TV sports comedy, taps into that zeitgeist by placing the Lady Greyhounds, a fictional women’s football team, at the heart of the show. This presents an opportunity and a challenge: pleasing old fans while welcoming new ones. Read more about why everyone’s watching.

Browse: A family-built, two-story boathouse in Ontario comes with a sauna.

Discover: This violinist and composer’s blazingly technical caprices are inspired by Kendrick Lamar and Nina Simone.

Drink: The Spaghett, Baltimore’s bright-red beer cocktail, has become a worldwide phenomenon.

Switch: I hate jeans. What can I wear instead?

The inspiration for this sesame soy chicken with garlic-scallion noodles comes from cha chaan teng, the noisy Hong Kong diners known for cheap meals and brusque service. The sauce is the engine here: Make it once and it keeps all week.

Where is this horse race?

Sanlúcar de Barrameda, Spain

Omey Island, Ireland

Montreal, Quebec

Waiheke Island, New Zealand

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

Amanda Taub was our guest writer today.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Harry and Meghan Will Move Back to Britain After 6 Years in U.S.
item.description:
Prince Harry, his wife, Meghan, and their children are moving back to Britain in the upcoming weeks, six years after moving to the United States amid a clash with other members of the royal family, according to two people familiar with his decision.

King Charles III was informed of the decision on Sunday, one of the people said, adding that the family’s move was not discussed when the Duke and Duchess of Sussex visited Britain and met with the king earlier this summer.

There will be no change in Harry and Meghan’s status as non-working royals, and they will remain as private individuals while they reside in Britain, both of the people said.

It was not clear where the family will live. The king welcomes the chance to spend more time with his younger son and his family, according to one of the people familiar with the move. Harry and Meghan have two children, Archie, 7 and Lilibet, 5.

One person said the duke and duchess have enrolled their children in school in time for them to start in September.

item.title: ‘No Interest’: North Korea Dismisses Reduced U.S. Drills With South Korea
item.description:
Kim Yo-jong, a powerful adviser and sister of North Korea’s leader, on Wednesday dismissed President Trump’s abrupt decision to scale back major military exercises with South Korea, saying the attempted overture “holds no interest for us.”

Ms. Kim, a spokeswoman for her brother Kim Jong-un’s government, said in a statement carried by state media that the reduced exercises were still “provocative and aggressive.”

She also said she was “unaware” of any communication between the governments in Pyongyang and Washington, contradicting President Trump’s claim on Tuesday that Mr. Kim had responded to his outreach.

Ms. Kim’s repudiation came amid Mr. Trump’s attempts to spur new talks with the North’s leader. On Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he expected to meet with Mr. Kim later this year.

Ms. Kim’s comments came one day after the Pentagon said it would end planned drills with South Korea one week earlier than scheduled. On Sunday, Mr. Trump ordered the Defense Department to reduce the 11-day training exercise, called Ulchi Freedom Shield.

U.S. allies in the region view the annual drills, a fixture of the decades-old security alliance between the United States and South Korea, as crucial to military preparedness and deterrence amid China’s expanding territorial ambitions and North Korea’s military posturing.

Under Mr. Kim, the North has not let up its nuclear weapons program. It has issued threats about its nuclear capabilities and conducted regular missile launch tests.

On Wednesday, the country’s state media channel, the Korean Central News Agency, carried an official statement denouncing the United States and South Korea as “warmongers” responsible for worsening tensions in the region through military exercises that it claimed had become increasingly aggressive each year.

North and South Korea are still technically at war, though the fighting paused after a 1953 armistice established the Demilitarized Zone between the two countries. Since then, the United States and South Korea have remained close military partners, though the relationship has been strained during Mr. Trump’s first and second terms.

Hanging over the tensions with South Korea is Mr. Trump’s inability to extract the United States from the war with Iran, now into its sixth month. His decision to reduce the military drills with South Korea was viewed as a way to punish that country for declining to join the war against Tehran.

Mr. Trump has appeared eager to move on from the conflict in the Middle East and pivot to dealing with Mr. Kim. At least twice in recent months, the American president posted a picture of himself with the North Korean leader on social media.

At summits during Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Kim had indulged Mr. Trump’s desire for leader-to-leader talks, but did not make any concessions on his country’s nuclear arsenal.

Mr. Trump’s overtures toward North Korea are not entirely unwelcome by his South Korean counterpart, President Lee Jae​ Myung, analysts said. A staunch proponent of inter-Korean reconciliation, Mr. Lee has urged Mr. Trump to ease tensions in the Korean Peninsula through direct talks with Mr. Kim. ​

North Korea has long cited the joint military drills as a major stumbling block to such efforts, calling them “a rehearsal for an aggressive war.”

item.title: U.A.E. Halts Trade Ties With Iran and Says It Was Targeted With Missiles
item.description:
The United Arab Emirates said it is halting all trade and financial transactions with Iran, increasing economic pressure on the Islamic Republic, hours after accusing Iran of launching ballistic missiles toward the Emirates.

The decision was made “in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security,” Afra Al Hameli, a spokeswoman for the Emirati Foreign Ministry, said in a statement late on Tuesday. She added that the Emirates was “firmly committed to safeguarding the integrity of the international financial system.”

The Emirates, located just 50 miles from Iran across the Persian Gulf, has nurtured close economic and cultural ties with the Islamic Republic for decades, despite political tensions between the two countries.

The Emirati city of Dubai has long been a major trade hub for Iran, and analysts say it has been key to Iranian efforts to evade sanctions — a fact that has often elicited complaints and pressure from American authorities. Emirati officials say that they crack down on any sanctions violations when they find them.

The Emirati government statement did not specify what prompted its announcement, nor did it make it clear when the decision to halt trade was implemented. But over the past week, the Emirates has accused Iran of attacking Emirati oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway on Iran’s southern coast that is a key transit route for oil and gas shipping.

And on Tuesday, the Emirati Defense Ministry issued warnings of an incoming missile attack, later saying that two ballistic missiles launched from Iran had targeted maritime aviation. Iran denied carrying out those attacks, and has neither denied nor claimed responsibility for the recent tanker strikes.

The decision to halt trade with Iran was announced hours after a call from President Trump to the Emirati ruler, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed.

After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, setting off a regional conflagration, the Emirates bore the initial brunt of Iran’s retaliation. The Emirates, which hosts a major American military base, reported more than 2,700 ballistic missile and drone attacks from Iran.

After the United States and Iran reached an initial cease-fire agreement in April, tensions between the Emirates and Iran had eased significantly, with direct contact between senior officials and the resumption of flights between the two countries.

As the truce has frayed in the months since, Iran largely focused its attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, sparing the Emirates.

The recent attacks on Emirati oil tankers have elicited a strong condemnation from the Emirati government, and on Saturday, the Emirati Foreign Ministry accused Iran of targeting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as “a tool of economic coercion or blackmail” that constituted a “direct threat to the stability of the region.”

In a call on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Emirates’ national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, discussed “U.S.-UAE coordination to hold Iran and its terrorist proxies accountable for ongoing attacks,” according to a state department spokesman, Tommy Pigott.

The Emirati Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the motivation and timing of its decision.

Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting from London.
